title: Docker Compose Complete Course
subtitle: Model, run and operate multi-container applications
description: Compose is the fastest path from a set of containers to a reproducible application. Learn the full specification: services, networks, volumes, configuration, health, profiles and production overrides.
outcomes: Read and write a complete compose.yaml
Model service dependencies and health checks
Manage configuration with env files, secrets and configs
Use profiles and override files for dev/prod workflows

modules.title: The Compose model
modules.summary: Files, projects and the command lifecycle.

lessons.title: Compose architecture and the file model
lessons.summary: A Compose file is a declarative description of a project. The CLI turns it into Docker API calls.
objectives: Explain the project model and naming
Know the difference between compose.yaml and docker-compose.yml

sections.title: One file, one project
sections.body:
Compose reads `compose.yaml` (preferred) or `docker-compose.yml`, resolves variables, validates the model, and creates a **project**. Resources are named `<project>_<resource>` by default, so two checkouts can run side by side with `-p`.

The top-level keys are `services`, `networks`, `volumes`, `secrets`, `configs`, `name`, and `include`. The obsolete top-level `version` key is ignored by modern Compose and should be removed.

sections.caption: Compose resolves the file into a project containing services, networks, volumes, secrets and configs.

sections.code:
name: acme

services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://app:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app -d app"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  pgdata:
sections.note: Modern Compose does not need a `version:` key. Use `docker compose config` to see the fully resolved model.

sections.title: Always validate before shipping
sections.body: `docker compose config --quiet` fails fast on syntax and interpolation errors and is ideal for CI.

exercises.title: Isolate projects
exercises.prompt: Run the same file twice under project names dev and test.
exercises.expected: Use -p dev and -p test; resources and containers are namespaced.

questions.question: What is the preferred default filename?
questions.explain: Compose prefers compose.yaml, though docker-compose.yml is still supported.

questions.question: What does the project name control?
questions.explain: Resources are prefixed with the project name.

questions.question: Is the top-level version key required?
questions.explain: Modern Compose ignores it and recommends removing it.

lessons.title: Services: image, build, ports and commands
lessons.summary: The service object is the heart of Compose. Learn the fields that define a container.
objectives: Use develop and watch for local workflows

sections.title: image or build
sections.body: A service either pulls an `image` or builds from a `build` context, or both (build and tag as the image). Use `build.context` plus `image` so the built result gets a stable name. `build.args` passes build-time values; they are visible in image history and must not contain secrets.

sections.code:
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
      target: runtime
      args:
        NODE_VERSION: "20"
    image: acme/api:local
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      LOG_LEVEL: ${LOG_LEVEL:-info}
    env_file:
      - path: .env
        required: false
    command: ["node", "dist/server.js"]
    working_dir: /app
    user: "1000:1000"
    restart: unless-stopped
    stop_grace_period: 30s
    init: true
sections.note: `${VAR:-default}` is Compose interpolation, not shell. `$$` escapes a literal dollar sign.

head: Field
Meaning
rows: Image reference to pull or tag
Map or list of env vars
Run a tiny init as PID 1

sections.title: Compose interpolation happens before containers start
sections.body: Values from your shell and `.env` are substituted into the file. If a variable is missing, Compose warns and substitutes an empty string. Use `${VAR:?error}` to fail fast.

questions.explain: `ports` creates host bindings; `expose` is internal documentation.

questions.question: Build args are appropriate for…

questions.question: What does ${VAR:-default} do?
options: Uses default when unset or empty

lessons.title: Networks and volumes in Compose
lessons.summary: Implicit defaults, explicit topologies, external resources and naming.

sections.title: Defaults and intent
sections.body:
Compose creates a default network named `<project>_default` and attaches every service to it. Services can reach each other by service name. Volumes referenced in services but not declared at top level are created as anonymous or project-scoped resources; declare them explicitly for control.

Use multiple networks to separate tiers: a frontend network for the proxy and app, a backend network for app and database. The database is then unreachable from the proxy.

sections.code:
services:
  proxy:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports: ["80:80"]
    networks: [frontend]
  api:
    build: .
    networks: [frontend, backend]
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    networks: [backend]
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data

networks:
  frontend:
  backend:
    internal: true

volumes:
  pgdata:
    name: acme_pgdata
sections.note: An internal network has no external connectivity; db can talk to api but cannot reach the internet.

sections.title: Name production volumes deliberately
sections.body: The `name:` field prevents accidental renames when the project name changes, which would otherwise create a new empty volume.

questions.question: What is the default Compose network called?
questions.explain: It is prefixed with the project name.

questions.question: What does internal: true do?
options: Removes external connectivity from the network
questions.explain: Internal networks have no gateway to outside networks.

questions.question: Why declare a volume name explicitly?
questions.explain: The name fixes the volume identity.

lessons.title: Environment, secrets and configs
lessons.summary: Configuration is not one thing. Separate ordinary settings, sensitive values and read-only config files.
objectives: Mount Compose secrets without baking them into images

sections.title: Three channels
sections.body:
**Environment**: ordinary configuration. Compose loads `.env` for interpolation and `env_file` for container environment. Values are visible in inspect.

**Secrets**: sensitive values mounted as files under `/run/secrets/<name>` by default. They are not in the image or environment.

**Configs**: non-secret files (nginx.conf, app config) mounted read-only, with the same declarative model.

sections.code:
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
    env_file:
      - .env
    secrets:
      - db_password
      - source: tls_key
        target: tls.key
        mode: 0400
    configs:
      - source: nginx_conf
        target: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt
  tls_key:
    environment: TLS_KEY

configs:
  nginx_conf:
    file: ./nginx.conf
sections.note: In a Swarm, secrets and configs are first-class; in Compose they are mounted files. Both keep secrets out of image layers.

sections.code:
# Read a secret inside the container
docker compose exec api sh -c 'cat /run/secrets/db_password'

# Check what Compose will run without starting it
docker compose config
sections.note: Do not print secrets in shared logs. This is for a local verification only.

sections.title: Environment variables are not secrets
sections.body: Anything in the environment is visible through inspect, /proc, crash dumps and child processes. Use secrets for credentials.

exercises.title: Secret mount
exercises.prompt: Declare a secret from ./secrets/db_password.txt and mount it in api.
exercises.expected: Top-level secrets + service secrets entry; verify with cat /run/secrets/db_password.

exercises.title: Env precedence
exercises.prompt: Explain the precedence between shell env, .env, env_file and the environment map.
exercises.expected: Shell/.env feed interpolation; env_file loads container values; the service environment map overrides env_file.

questions.question: Where does a Compose secret appear in the container?
questions.explain: Secrets are mounted as files by default.

questions.question: What is .env used for?
questions.explain: Compose reads .env for variable substitution; env_file sets container env.

lessons.title: Health checks and dependencies
lessons.summary: depends_on only controls start order unless you attach a health condition. Learn the difference between started and ready.

sections.title: Started is not ready
sections.body:
By default `depends_on` waits for the dependency container to start, not for its application to accept connections. A database process can be running while still initialising. Use a health check plus `condition: service_healthy` to wait for readiness.

Compose does not restart a dependent service when a dependency later becomes unhealthy. For resilient systems, the application must also retry connections.

sections.code:
services:
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
      cache:
        condition: service_started
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 12
      start_period: 5s
  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 5
sections.note: `start_period` gives slow starters time before failures count.

sections.title: Health checks can lie
sections.body: A TCP check only proves the port is open. Use an application-level endpoint that verifies dependencies when readiness matters.

questions.question: What does depends_on do by default?
questions.explain: Without a condition it only orders startup.

questions.question: Which condition waits for a health check?
questions.explain: service_healthy waits for the health check to pass.

questions.question: What is start_period for?
options: Delaying the first retry accounting for startup
questions.explain: It gives slow applications time before failures count.

lessons.title: Profiles, overrides and production
lessons.summary: One project, several contexts: development, testing, production and optional tooling.
objectives: Use profiles to opt into services
Run Compose safely in production-like deployments

sections.title: Profiles are opt-in service groups
sections.body: A service with `profiles: ["debug"]` does not start unless the profile is enabled with `--profile debug` or `COMPOSE_PROFILES`. Services without profiles always start. Use profiles for admin tools, seeders, test runners and optional databases.

sections.code:
# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    image: acme/api:1.4
  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
  adminer:
    image: adminer:4
    profiles: ["debug"]
    ports: ["8081:8080"]
  test:
    build: { context: ., target: test }
    profiles: ["test"]
    command: npm test
sections.note: `docker compose --profile debug up -d` starts api, db and adminer.

sections.title: Overrides
sections.body: Compose merges multiple `-f` files in order. Put shared definition in `compose.yaml`, production-specific settings in `compose.prod.yaml`, and run `docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d`. Lists such as `ports` are appended for some fields; understand merge rules before relying on them.

sections.code:
# validate the merged model
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml config

# production-like run
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml pull
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --wait

# stop and remove, keeping volumes
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml down
sections.note: `--wait` waits for services to be healthy before returning, if health checks are defined.

sections.title: Compose is not a cluster scheduler
sections.body: A single-host Compose deployment has no rescheduling, rolling update or multi-node failover. Use Swarm, Kubernetes or a managed platform when you need those guarantees.
